deep_why: Generative recommenders score items one-at-a-time as they produce text, but each choice reinforces patterns already seen in the user's history—the system depends most heavily on early tokens to steer what comes next. The root issue is that this sequential anchoring amplifies even small preference biases: if history points slightly toward action movies, the system will lean harder toward that genre with each new item it suggests. Deeper reasoning with more varied information sources interrupts this cycle, because different signals (user's seasonal moods, social circles, past dislikes) can pull the recommendation in fresh directions and correct for what the raw history would naively suggest. By reasoning longer before committing to each item and drawing on richer signals at each step, the system avoids tunneling into a narrow band of similar recommendations—the real problem users face when suggestions feel repetitive despite diverse taste.

Detecting harmful video content requires separating actual harm signals from false alarms; the challenge is that any single clue—a harsh word, a violent image, an angry tone—can appear without harmful intent. The method treats each signal (text, sound, image, metadata) as independent evidence and asks which signals agree about whether harm exists. This works because genuine harmful content tends to show the same story across multiple channels: if the video's words, visuals, and audio all point the same direction, that convergence is far stronger proof than any one piece alone. Absence of a signal in one channel (for instance, the video has no script) doesn't damage the reasoning—it simply means that channel contributes no vote. By making the decision process transparent (showing which evidence tipped the scale) and deterministic (always following the same logic rules), the system earns trust from moderators and platforms who must defend their safety choices, while correctly flagging truly harmful content over accidental matches.

Mobile agents fail when they encounter unfamiliar apps because they lack the playbook for how each app's buttons and workflows actually work—they have to guess and fumble. The method detects when the agent is stuck or uncertain (scoring its own doubt during task execution) and retrieves structured documentation about the app before trying again. This works because when an agent knows the rules—which parameter belongs in which field, how to navigate between screens, what each button typically does—it can make smarter decisions about what action to take next rather than exploring randomly. The documentation is organized to highlight the semantic meaning of interactions (not just pixel-level details), so the agent can reason about whether a button is for saving versus canceling, creating space for thoughtful planning instead of trial-and-error. By grounding uncertainty in explicit retrieval of domain knowledge, the agent trades pure generalization for practical reliability in real smartphone tasks.

Predicting future events from news text requires extracting two kinds of clues from the past: what happened before shapes what comes next (temporal chains), and multiple related stories happening together often point to a common cause (correlations within the same moment). The method reasons backward along the timeline to spot trends and forward across documents to find hidden connections between seemingly separate facts. This works because real-world events don't spring from nowhere—they build on previous conditions and often triggered by multiple converging factors that the text signals separately. By reasoning both backward and sideways, the system avoids the trap of forcing events into simple linear chains (which misses feedback loops) while also catching the subtle associations that single-document analysis would overlook. Adding self-checking, where the system verifies its own inferences against what the documents actually say, prevents confidently predicting events that contradict the evidence—the real failure mode that harms trust in forecasts.

Robots act by aligning visual inputs with language instructions to pick the right motion—an attacker can inject tiny image changes (imperceptible to humans) that break this alignment without the robot noticing something is wrong. The method crafts perturbations that deliberately disrupt how the different modalities (image and instruction) co-activate in the robot's model, pushing them to disagree about what action to take. This works because the model learned to trust that vision and language should agree on the task; when an adversary breaks that agreement in targeted regions, the model's decision flips even though the image looks nearly identical. Balancing attack strength against visual stealth (small enough that humans dismiss it as noise) is critical because a visible attack is useless in practice—the deployment person or safety system would catch it. By showing this vulnerability exists and can remain hidden, the work motivates robot designers to check for robust agreement between modalities, not just high accuracy in one channel alone.

Detecting attacks on autonomous vehicles over satellite links requires processing signals from dozens of sensors, communication channels, and control signals fast enough to respond before the vehicle crashes—but cloud processing is too slow over satellite. The method fuses these signals at the edge (on the vehicle itself) and uses basic physical laws as a check: an attack that tells the steering wheel to turn 180 degrees while moving at highway speed is physically impossible, so it can be dismissed without further thought. This works because legitimate sensor readings and commands obey the laws of physics (momentum, gear ratios, electrical power limits), whereas injected attacks often violate those constraints. By filtering out attacks that break physical rules before doing expensive reasoning about the sensor details, the system saves computation and responds faster. Cross-checking that multiple signal channels agree (CAN bus, wireless communication, motion sensors) reinforces the confidence that a threat is real, not a blip in one sensor, making the detection both fast and trustworthy for safety-critical decisions.

Finding bugs in web applications when you can only see the surface (HTML, network responses) is hard because traditional test feedback tells you nothing—you don't know what code paths your inputs actually touched. The method infers hidden clues from the server's responses: change in page layout, presence of error messages, different content returned—these patterns hint at which parts of the code the input exercised. This works because different code paths produce different effects that users and testers can observe, even without seeing the code; the fuzzer learns to recognize these patterns and generates new inputs likely to trigger unexplored paths. Once paths are discovered, the fuzzer shifts strategy to try to exploit what it found (push error conditions harder, combine inputs in specific ways) rather than keep searching—this saves effort by specializing the attack once you know the terrain. By orchestrating two distinct strategies (broad exploration followed by targeted exploitation) guided by feedback signals mined from observable responses, the system finds real vulnerabilities that static checkers and random testing would miss.

E-commerce ranking must satisfy multiple goals simultaneously (selling products, keeping users engaged, encouraging deeper browsing), but these goals naturally conflict—a high-profit item might bore users, and an engaging recommendation might not sell. The method ranks items considering both which recommendations help across all these goals together and which sequences of recommendations work well over multiple steps. This works because users make sequential decisions, and optimizing each step independently (myopic ranking) can trap you in low-value paths early, whereas planning ahead prevents short-term tradeoffs from blocking long-term goals. By pushing the boundary of what's simultaneously achievable (frontier optimization), the system avoids choosing items that sacrifice all goals for one and avoids getting stuck in temporal ruts where each slot's best local choice prevents later slots from doing well. Applied to the full-screen browsing experience where users swipe through many items fast, multi-step planning is essential because a mediocre first recommendation colors all subsequent user engagement and willingness to buy.

Federated learning trains models across many devices without centralizing data, but devices have different data distributions, so using one shared feature representation (prototype) for each category fails—your local data might use different visual aspects to recognize 'dog' than mine. The method breaks down class prototypes into reusable semantic building blocks (visual primitives) that can be shared and recombined, so each device adapts them to its own distribution. This works because real-world categories are compositional: 'dog' is built from parts (texture, shape, color patterns) that appear across many classes and devices, enabling cross-category and cross-device knowledge transfer. By decomposing instead of treating each class as monolithic, you need far fewer centralized parameters, reducing communication burden. Adding language as a bridge (text descriptions that ground what each primitive means) lets each device reinterpret shared primitives through its own data without requiring everyone to retrain together—language provides the semantic anchor that makes reuse reliable even when local visual distributions differ.

Graph neural networks must adapt as the data they operate on evolves—new entities arrive, relationships shift, and old patterns become obsolete. Learning everything continuously leads to catastrophic forgetting where the network discards old knowledge trying to master the new. The method routes parameter updates through a state-space controller that compresses the current domain into a compact summary, then decodes that summary into small adapter parameters injected into the frozen base network. This works because the base model's learned features remain stable while only thin adapter layers change per domain, creating a buffer that prevents violent erasure of old knowledge. The state space itself evolves through time, capturing how domains shift gradually rather than treating each update as independent; this continuity prevents the network from ping-ponging between old and new solutions. By penalizing adapter changes between time steps and maintaining unsupervised information gain, the system provably avoids catastrophic forgetting while staying lightweight—the old knowledge stays in the frozen base, the new domain shifts are captured in thin, time-aware adapter layers.

Locating users from sparse social media data is hard because user information is heterogeneous and noisy—one user's posts mention places vaguely, another drops GPS hints, a third tweets mainly about distant friends. The method aligns user profiles and geographic locations in a shared semantic space by learning which users and places are similar based on limited labeled examples. This works because users and places have latent structure: people in the same region tend to share interests, language patterns, and social circles, even if no single post confirms it. By treating this as a matching problem and mining hard examples (users or places that are easy to confuse), the system learns to emphasize the distinctions that matter, rather than spreading attention equally. Adding language prompts (descriptions of places, patterns of user behavior) as external knowledge anchors the learned space to human-interpretable geography, preventing spurious similarities. Combining these forces—contrastive learning from examples plus semantic grounding from language—solves few-shot geolocation by making maximum use of each labeled user-location pair.

Sequential recommenders produce personalized explanations by reasoning from a user's past choices to justify why a new item fits, but sparse data means explanations are often generic or repeat. The method aggregates textual information from past items (user reviews, product descriptions, attributes) and fuses this rich history with traditional collaborative patterns. This works because explanations are more persuasive and specific when grounded in concrete details from what users actually chose, not abstract user-item relations; textual information provides the specificity that makes an explanation feel tailored rather than templated. Different fusion strategies (merging text early versus late in reasoning) control when text influences the model—early fusion lets text shape overall representation, late fusion lets it refine the final explanation without overwhelming collaborative signals. By auditing which text aggregation and fusion methods preserve recommendation quality while enhancing explanation richness, the system finds the right balance between personalization depth and model stability, letting explanations be both truthful to the recommendation logic and compelling to the reader.

Large language models excel at reasoning about user preferences but fail when confronted with long sequences (can't store the full history) and generate convincing but false preferences (hallucinations that sound plausible but contradict actual user behavior). The method segments long histories into chunks, infers preferences for each chunk, then uses the user's actual next action as a training signal: if the inferred preference wrongly predicted what the user did next, reinforcement learning penalizes that inference. This works because human behavior is the ground truth—if your preference model predicted the user would buy action movies but they bought romance, your model hallucinated; using real subsequent behavior as a reward signal forces the model to align with demonstrated intent. Reasoning sequentially over segments, rather than all at once, fits within memory limits and allows preference patterns to evolve naturally through time. Aggregating these chunk-level preferences into a dynamic long-term model with special learned functions for how preferences change prevents simple averaging from washing out important shifts in taste. This combination—segmentation plus reinforcement alignment plus temporal modeling—recovers predictive fidelity by tethering each preference inference to what the user actually does next.

Knowledge graphs grow over time as new facts are discovered, but retraining embeddings from scratch wastes computation and can overwrite representations of old entities and relations that were working well. The method initializes embeddings for new entities by borrowing information from related entities already in the graph (rather than guessing randomly), then updates all embeddings incrementally while measuring how much old knowledge persists and how much new knowledge is acquired. This works because related entities in a knowledge graph share semantic structure—a new person typically inherits some properties from people in similar roles or domains, giving a smarter starting point than random initialization. Tracking forgetting and learning explicitly (instead of just watching accuracy) lets practitioners tune when to update, how to prioritize old versus new facts, and whether the model is drifting away from established truths. Extending a working library like PyKEEN with continual learning support means practitioners can reuse models and training recipes instead of rebuilding from scratch, making continual updates a practical deployment option.

Predicting whether a student can solve a programming problem requires understanding their knowledge state, but programming answers are messier than traditional homework—they give partial credit based on test cases passed, contain logical errors independent of domain knowledge, and demand reasoning skills separate from concept recall. The method analyzes submission code to find root causes of failures (off-by-one errors, logic flaws, misconceptions) and labels each submission with multiple layers of meaning (which concepts apply, what reasoning went wrong, how severe the error). This works because a traditional binary correct/wrong label loses information—two students both fail, but one misunderstood a concept and one made a typo. By decomposing failures into semantic layers, the model can distinguish real knowledge gaps from noise in noisy test-case scores. Using language models to automate this analysis scales the work to large student populations. The multi-level model then tracks evolution of knowledge across three dimensions (concepts, reasoning, techniques) rather than assuming performance on one problem tells you everything about a student's progress, giving tutoring systems the signal they need to offer targeted help rather than generic practice.
